The mini electric dirt bike market has exploded over the last few years, with seemingly countless new brands offering everything from pint-sized electric pit bikes to surprisingly powerful off-road machines. The Sykeruns X7 falls somewhere in the middle, offering enough power to get into some serious trouble while keeping the price relatively approachable.
I’ve spent some time now riding the X7, and while it certainly isn’t the most refined electric dirt bike I’ve tested, there’s enough to like about what you’re getting for the money.
In fact, if you’re looking for a reasonably powerful electric dirt bike for recreational trail riding without spending several thousand dollars, this might be worth a closer look.
Sykeruns X7: What are we working with here?
The Sykeruns X7 is a compact electric dirt bike featuring a 5,500W peak-rated motor, which translates to around 7.4 horsepower. That’s quite a bit of power for a bike at this price point of $1,699 , especially considering that many similarly priced electric two-wheelers are significantly less powerful. Oh, and for our readers, we’ve gotten you set up with a 20% discount. Just use code ELECTREK20 to drop the price down to an impressive $1,359!
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Sykeruns claims a top speed of 57 mph (92 km/h), though since this is an off-road only bike, you’ll rarely get the chance to put that claim to the test. I certainly didn’t, as I didn’t have a long enough and flat enough stretch of trail where I felt comfortable hitting nearly highway speeds on a low-cost e-moto.
The battery is a 60V 27Ah pack, providing 1,620 Wh of capacity. Sykeruns claims up to 60 miles (96 km) of range, though as with virtually every electric dirt bike, your actual range will depend heavily on how aggressively you’re riding. Fast trail riding, steep climbs, and repeated hard acceleration can eat through battery capacity much more quickly than leisurely cruising. Suffice it to say that you’ll likely not see the 60 mile figure in real world scenarios, but that’s still a fairly large battery.
The bike rolls on a 17-inch front wheel and 14-inch rear wheel, both wrapped in knobby off-road tires. Hydraulic disc brakes handle stopping duties, while an inverted suspension fork and rear monoshock help smooth out the bumps.
At 143 lb (65 kg), the X7 isn’t exactly featherweight, but it’s also far from being a full-size electric motorcycle.
How does the Sykeruns X7 actually ride?
The first thing I was surprised about with the X7 is that it offers a pretty decent amount of performance for the money. There’s enough power here to have some real fun, and the bike doesn’t feel like one of those underpowered mini electric motorcycles that struggles once you get beyond casual neighborhood speeds.
That said, I wouldn’t describe the acceleration as mind-blowing, either. We’re not talking about the kind of explosive power delivery you’d get from a high-end electric dirt bike costing several times as much. Instead, the X7 delivers a healthy amount of acceleration that feels appropriate for a recreational off-road machine.
And let’s be real here, that’s probably what most people shopping in this budget category are looking for.
The suspension is another area where the X7 earns a passing grade without necessarily winning any awards. The front fork and rear shock do their jobs, absorbing the bumps and ruts you’d expect to encounter on typical trails. It’s nothing I’d call plush, but I could see it doing light jumps with minimal air time.
Would I want to take this thing to a motocross track and start launching it off massive jumps? Not particularly. The suspension doesn’t have the premium feel or sophisticated damping of more expensive machines.
But for general trail riding, exploring dirt roads, and the occasional overlanding shenanigans, it’s perfectly serviceable. Not every electric dirt bike needs to be a competition-ready machine, and the X7 seems comfortable occupying that more recreational category.
I was also pleasantly surprised by the tires, which seem well suited to the bike’s intended purpose. The knobby tread offers a reasonable amount of grip for off-road riding, and I didn’t find myself immediately wishing for a tire upgrade.
The overall size is worth mentioning, too. This isn’t a particularly large electric dirt bike, but at my modest 5’7” (170 cm) height, I felt comfortable on it. The riding position didn’t feel overly cramped, and the bike was manageable enough that I didn’t feel like I was wrestling with an oversized machine.
Taller riders might find it a bit more compact than they’d prefer, but for average-height riders, the proportions seem reasonable.
Build quality: Good enough, but nothing extraordinary
If there’s one area where the X7 reminds you of its budget-friendly $1,699 price tag, it’s the overall level of refinement.
Nothing about the bike struck me as particularly premium. The components, finishes, and general construction are more in line with what I’d expect from a relatively inexpensive electric dirt bike.
But that’s not necessarily a criticism. There’s a difference between something feeling inexpensive and something feeling inadequate, and the X7 generally stays on the acceptable side of that line.
The controls are straightforward, the digital display provides the basic information you need, and the overall package feels focused on delivering usable performance rather than impressing riders with fancy features.
The grippy hydraulic brakes are also a welcome inclusion, especially considering the speeds this bike is capable of reaching. With a machine that can approach highway speeds, having proper motorcycle-style braking hardware is important.
Of course, long-term durability is a separate question. Budget electric dirt bikes don’t always have the same track record, parts availability, or established dealer networks as the more recognizable motorcycle brands. That’s something worth considering before purchasing, particularly if you plan to ride hard or frequently.
One important warning: This is NOT a street-legal e-bike
One thing I appreciate about the Sykeruns X7 is that the company makes its intended use fairly clear.
There’s a large red warning sticker on the bike explaining that it’s intended for off-road use only. That’s a good thing, especially in today’s market, where the lines between electric bicycles, electric dirt bikes, and electric motorcycles are becoming increasingly blurred, despite laws existing to keep these types of bikes out of the bike lane and off of public roads.
The X7 is absolutely not an electric bicycle. It doesn’t have pedals, it produces several thousand watts of power, and it’s capable of speeds far beyond anything permitted under electric bicycle regulations.
It’s an off-road electric motorcycle, plain and simple.
Interestingly, though, Sykeruns has equipped the bike with features like a tail light and turn signals, which could potentially give some riders the wrong impression.
Those are certainly useful features on a motorcycle, but they don’t magically make a vehicle street legal. Without the necessary certification, registration, and other road-use requirements, the X7 remains an off-road-only machine.
I worry that some buyers might see those lights and assume they can ride the bike around town like a small electric motorcycle. That’s not the case, and it’s important to understand that distinction before buying one.
Electrek’s Take
After spending time with the Sykeruns X7, my biggest takeaway is that this is a reasonably capable electric dirt bike at a pretty compelling price.
It’s not the best electric dirt bike I’ve ever ridden. The suspension is fairly basic, the build quality is unremarkable, and there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about the design.
But for $1,699 (or $1,359 if you use the code ELECTREK20 to take 20% off!), you’re getting a 5.5 kW peak-rated electric motorcycle with a sizable battery, proper off-road tires, hydraulic brakes, and enough performance to have some genuine fun on the trails.
That’s not a bad deal.
I wouldn’t say that the X7 here is trying to compete with more up-market electric dirt bikes from the likes of Juiced, Sur-Ron or Talaria on overall refinement, but they make this type of riding much more accessible.
And that’s really where I think the X7 makes the most sense.
If you’re an experienced dirt bike rider looking for a highly refined machine with excellent suspension and premium components, you’ll probably want to keep shopping.
But if you’re someone who wants a fun electric dirt bike for exploring private property, cruising around trails where motorized riding is permitted, or just enjoying some recreational off-road riding without spending a fortune, the Sykeruns X7 offers a pretty reasonable package.
It doesn’t need to be amazing at everything. At this price, being pretty good at most things is already an accomplishment.

As AI tools multiply across freight and logistics, the important question is how much control to hand over, and to what. On the latest Lean Quarterly Dive, host Malcolm Harris sat down with Lean Solutions Group CTO Alfonso Quijano to unpack that question. “experts in the loop,” a model that treats human judgment
Quijano didn’t waste time getting to the thesis. “Experts in the loop,” according to Quijano, is a model that treats human judgment not as a stopgap for AI’s limitations, but as the thing that makes AI worth using in the first place.
“Experts in the loop is the natural evolution of the logistics roles inside of every operation for every broker and every logistics player,” Quijano said. AI has unlocked real productivity gains across the industry, he said, but its full value only shows up once it’s paired with human judgment.
“You don’t really leverage its full capabilities until you pair it up with the right judgment and the right capabilities that come from a human expert,” Quijano explained, adding that Lean isn’t interested in building a world where AI makes decisions unsupervised. Instead, the model splits the work. AI handles the repetitive grunt work, while humans stay in the loop feeding it judgment so it keeps improving and can be trusted with the harder calls.
Standard operating procedures are still in a process of development as AI becomes integrated into more and more workflows. According to Quijano, most companies have never made SOPs usable by AI in a way that tightens the feedback loop. When an AI system hits a case the SOP doesn’t cover well, an expert needs to confirm there’s an operational gap before the document gets updated. Right now, most SOPs are static, reviewed once and then forgotten.
Quijano drew a comparison here that’s likely to resonate with anyone who’s spent time inside modern AI tooling: the CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md files that let AI agents share context and coordinate with each other.
“What Anthropic and OpenAI and all these guys have figured out is that for the agents to work together and understand everything, they need to have a file where they write all the things that they’re doing in order to improve and get better,” Quijano said, noting that the concept is functionally identical to an SOP. It acts as a living source of truth for how a process works and how it evolves. Quijano believes that SOPs are headed in that direction industry-wide, and that they will be updated far more frequently by both AI and the people who oversee it in a feedback loop that will reshape how operational knowledge gets maintained.
The market is still determining where AI earns its keep today and where it falls short. Quijano’s list of clear use cases include document-heavy workflows such as invoice intake, discrepancy checks against bills of lading, routing emails to the right agent, and the kind of accounts-payable and accounts-receivable work.
These are tasks where fatigue and inattention cause real human error, and there’s a tradeoff.
“The AI is not going to miss,” Quijano said. “At least the accuracy for the AI is much higher in those cases.”
Quijano described the typical handoff point as built around dollar thresholds and client-specific rules. An invoice might suddenly include a batch of unfamiliar accessorial fees and get flagged for a human to verify, and that person’s decision then trains the system on whether to treat similar cases as exceptions going forward or adjust the threshold entirely.
Carrier sales tell a different story. “I’m bullish on the potential for the technology,” Quijano said, but he’s more cautious about full autonomy, largely because of what gets lost when a human isn’t involved in the early stages of a client relationship.
Trust is something AI still can’t deliver on its own. That’s generated through the human parts of sales and first contact that are harder to automate. He drew a distinction between inbound carrier sales, where a lot of spot-market inquiry volume is low-value noise AI can reasonably triage, and outbound sales, where the calculus is murkier and companies are still figuring out whether to go all-in or ease into automation gradually.
“Decision intelligence,” as Quijano described it, is Lean’s attempt to combine 14 years of operational knowledge with an AI layer that behaves like an embedded assistant, whether that’s in the format of a sidebar, desktop app, or always-on presence that watches for ambiguous data or risky decisions in real time and flags them before they become problems.
New hires at Lean, Quijano said, would typically route around half their tasks to a manager on day one. With decision intelligence pulling from SOPs, operational history and peer behavior to suggest next steps automatically, that onboarding drag shrinks dramatically.
Across document-based automations specifically, Quijano cited figures in the range of 65 to 70 hours of time given back to operators per month, or roughly a quarter of their working hours. But that gain isn’t pure profit. A share of that reclaimed time gets reinvested into training and giving feedback to the AI systems themselves, which is a necessary cost of the model, according to Quijano.
Asked what advice he’d give a logistics executive weighing how to bring AI into their operation without losing control, security or sound judgment, Quijano said that step one is mapping the business down to atomic-level workflows to identify where exceptions live and where automation makes sense.
Lean can benchmark that distinction against data from across its own client base rather than leaving companies to guess in isolation. Step two is understanding where a given AI tool sits on the autonomy spectrum, from simple rules-based (“deterministic”) processes up through fully agentic systems that can retain memory, deploy tools independently and act on what they observe. Not every workflow, he stressed, needs to be agentic. Plenty of companies are forcing agentic complexity onto processes that would run just fine on simpler, more predictable logic.
The last piece, according to Quijano, is planning for the share of the workload that stays human. In Lean’s experience, AI typically handles 70% to 80% of a given process, leaving the remaining 20% to 30% as exception management that requires trained people, many of whom are now operating in a different role. Rather than running the core process, those experts become coaches and ambassadors for the AI itself, reinforcing good outcomes and supplying evidence when something goes wrong.
“That’s the next challenge,” Quijano said. “That shift matters just as much as the technology decisions.”
Lean Solution Group will demo at F3, and Quijano says that much of this topic will be on display.
In addition, Leans Solutions Group recently announced the release of new Everest Group research showing that enterprises are adopting artificial intelligence much faster than they are redesigning operations to realize AI’s full business value. The report, “Designing the Human + AI Enterprise: A Transformation Agenda for Supply Chain-Intensive Industries ,” is being introduced in conjunction with the FreightWaves F3 event, October 26–28, in Chattanooga, TN. A webinar will be hosted with an Everest Group analyst on December 8 to discuss the research and noteworthy insights for the industry.
For more information on Lean’s platforms, including decision intelligence and its Agent Edge product, visit leangroup.com .

FreightWaves revealed the 2027 FreightTech 25 at the inaugural F3 Awards Dinner in Chattanooga, where all 100 FreightTech 100 winners were recognized as part of the 2027 FreightTech Awards, presented by Sope Creek . Kevin Nolan, Craig Fuller and Malcolm Harris closed the evening by announcing the top 25.
The list recognizes 25 companies for their contributions to innovation across freight technology and transportation. Highway claimed the No. 1 spot for the third consecutive year, tying the record Amazon set from 2019 to 2021.
The Dallas-based company develops technology that helps freight brokers verify trucking companies, prevent cargo theft and fraud, and find reliable carriers for loads. Its platform checks carrier identity, operating authority, insurance and operational data, while its Trusted Freight Exchange connects brokers with verified capacity.
“I think there’s been no bigger story over the last decade,” Fuller said of the rise of fraud and cargo theft prevention technology.
The FreightTech 25
The FreightTech 25 is selected from the FreightTech 100 , a broader list of 100 companies recognized by FreightWaves for innovation in freight and supply chain technology. An independent panel ranks the 100 companies to determine the top 25, with the voting process overseen by accounting firm Henderson, Hutcherson & McCullough.
Highway and GenLogs’ top finishes put freight fraud prevention at the forefront of this year’s rankings. Highway focuses on verifying carrier identities, while GenLogs uses highway camera networks and data to help verify carriers and track freight capacity.
Artificial intelligence was another major theme. Five companies in the AI orchestration and automation category made the list: HappyRobot, CloneOps.ai, Augment, Pallet and Carrier1. All five are first-time FreightTech 25 winners.
The companies reflect a shift toward AI tools that can carry out work, rather than simply assist employees. C.H. Robinson, which ranked No. 11, said its AI fully executes 92% of shipments for customers that outsource their transportation operations.
Autonomous trucking was also highlighted, with four companies making this year’s list, up from three last year. Aurora ranked No. 4, Kodiak AI came in at No. 12, Torc Robotics ranked No. 19 and Waabi placed No. 20.
The list also included fewer traditional transportation providers. Eight carriers, brokers and third-party logistics providers made the 2026 FreightTech 25, compared with just two this year: C.H. Robinson and Amazon Relay.

source_document.body:
The nation’s electric grid depends heavily on foreign-made equipment, much of it from China. Depending on how the Dept. of Energy (DOE) chooses to implement Executive Order 14421 through its pending rulemaking for national security purposes, it has the potential to prohibit fully any Chinese-made equipment on the transmission grid.
COMMENTARY
The significance of Executive Order 14421 cannot be overstated. For owners, operators, lenders, and builders, the question now is how to manage the risk while the rules take shape. That could be disastrous for efforts to maintain and build out the system, not only for load growth but for existing load.
A Rule is Coming, But Its Scope is Unknown
Signed Aug. 26, 2026, the Executive Order invokes the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to declare a national emergency over the foreign supply of bulk-power system (a k a transmission) equipment and allows the Secretary of Energy to prohibit the acquisition, importation, transfer, or installation of foreign-produced equipment tied to a “Covered Foreign Entity.”
That category at its core includes Chinese entities. The prohibition applies notwithstanding existing contracts, licenses, or permits. Covered equipment is defined broadly to include items in substations, control rooms, and generating stations, as well as transmission level transformers, breakers, turbines, generators, relays, industrial control systems, grid-connected inverters, and battery storage.
Nothing is prohibited until the acts. Its implementing rules are due by Dec. 24, 2026, and will determine which equipment and manufacturers are covered and what licensing path exists. Until then, the industry is managing a risk with no defined edges. Here’s where we believe potential exposure sits:
Supply chain and schedule risk. Long-lead equipment is already hard to source. A prohibition without a workable transition could strand orders and delay interconnection and commercial operation, triggering delay damages, change-in-law disputes, and covenant pressure.
Installed-base risk. The DOE may impose conditions on equipment already in service, from monitoring and isolation through replacement or removal, after weighing reliability and the availability of secure replacements. For operators, that is an operational question as much as a compliance one.
Contract and financing risk. Because the Executive Order can override existing agreements, supply contracts, EPC agreements, and financing documents should be reviewed for how they allocate regulatory risk. Who bears the cost if a covered item cannot be delivered or installed? Do representations, covenants, and conditions precedent account for that possibility?
Enforcement risk. IEEPA civil penalties can reach the greater of an inflation-adjusted amount exceeding $375,000 per violation or twice the transaction value, and willful violations carry criminal exposure. The Executive Order also prohibits evasion. Diligence must look past the manufacturer’s nameplate to subcomponents, software, and remote-access capabilities.
The Executive Order does include an important qualification, the breadth of which is currently unclear. Equipment produced, manufactured or assembled in the U.S., even if the manufacturer has a Chinese parent, falls outside the scope of the Executive Order—but it’s not clear how broadly or narrowly this qualification will be interpreted. It also contemplates mitigation agreements, which may resemble those used in CFIUS reviews. Companies that engage early and can anticipate potential mitigation measures will be better positioned.
What To Do Now
The Executive Order’s scope will not be known until DOE acts, but the exposure it addresses is knowable today. The right first step depends on where you sit. Owners and operators should inventory installed and ordered equipment, identify assets within scope of the Executive Order, which would be hardest to isolate or replace without affecting reliability, and potential mitigation measures in the event an installed item or item on order is designated.
Lenders and investors should conduct diligence that reaches subcomponents and software, and ensure that loan and acquisition documents address regulatory changes in either force majeure or change-in-law provisions. Contractors and developers should review delivery obligations, change-in-law provisions, and substitution rights before any items get designated and delay a project schedule.
— Jeffrey Jakubiak is a partner at Vinson & Elkins advising clients on FERC and energy regulatory matters from the firm’s New York and Washington, D.C., offices. Randall V. Johnston is a partner at Vinson & Elkins in Washington, D.C., who leads the firm’s CFIUS practice and advises on national security matters.

Nobody Wants This 2026 Ford Mustang Dark Horse SC for MSRP, Owner Turns Down $114,000 Offer
20 photos
Photo: Bring a Trailer/autoevolution
I'm of two minds when it comes to the Dark Horse SC. On the one hand, it's a proper performance car. Vastly superior to the "base" Dark Horse. On the other hand, it doesn't have the GTD's full chassis sophistication and engineering. In other words, the Dark Horse SC is merely an upgraded version of the conventional Mustang, whereas the GTD is a completely different beast.
We're talking a rear-mounted gearbox and a racing-derived pushrod system at the rear for the latter. It's pretty much a race car for the road, and therein lies the difference. I wouldn't use this as an explanation for why this car didn't sell, though. Its original sticker price was $118,085, and the bidding stopped at $114,000 - roughly 3.5% below sticker. Not enough to hit the reserve and generate a sale.
With 26 miles on the clock, this is still brand-new, so I wouldn't call what just happened here depreciation. It's a clear case of unmet expectations. Whether those expectations were realistic or not, that remains to be seen. Also, this isn't a limited-production car, as Ford hasn't announced a production cap. Nor have they disclosed how many examples are to be made.
I'm just as curious as you guys are with regards to the valuation . I think we need more data before we can officially call it one way or another. But the fact that someone tried to land it for below MSRP does make me think that there will be some depreciation on these cars, and possibly sooner rather than later.
Now, in terms of specs, there a lot to admire here , from the SC fender badging to the revised front fascia, model-specific vented hood, functional hood pins, underbody and rear diffuser, quad-exhaust outlets, Gurney flap rear spoiler... plus you get the exposed carbon fiber front grille, rear diffuser and mirror caps - courtesy of the $10k Carbon Fiber Exterior Package.
Meanwhile, the 20" Tarnished Dark Anodized alloy wheels are rocking Pirelli P Zero rubber, with stopping power provided by Notorious Blue six-piston front and four-piston rear Brembo calipers.
Photo: Bring a Trailer Moving along to the interior, that's where you'll find the Black Onyx ActiveX upholstery, a power-adjustable driver's seat, a 12-speaker Bang & Olufsen sound system, Ford Racing sill plates, sat-nav, cruise control, dual-zone automatic climate control, a leather-wrapped steering wheel, and more. As you can see, everything is wrapped in plastic. This car has likely never been driven (only moved).
The cherry on top is the supercharged 5.2-liter Predator cross-plane crank V8, same one as in the Mustang GTD. It sends 795 horsepower and 660 lb-ft of torque to the rear wheels via a Tremec dual-clutch automatic transmission. On paper, you should be able to hit 60 mph (97 kph) in about 2.9 - 3.0 seconds, making the Dark Horse SC about 0.5 seconds quicker to 60 than the 760-horsepower Shelby GT500 .

Shein has agreed to pay $100 million to settle a Federal Trade Commission investigation into delivery delays and other customer complaints, Reuters reported. The payment would equal 44% of the fast-fashion retailer ’s second-quarter profit.
What’s Related
Consumers filed more than 12,000 complaints about Shein involving purchases worth more than $11 million between January 2020 and June 2026, according to FTC records. Some customers said packages marked as delivered never arrived and that customer service did not resolve their complaints.
Shein, founded in China and headquartered in Singapore, told Reuters it had “reached a constructive outcome with the FTC” and would share more information soon. An FTC spokesperson declined to comment.
The company had warned in July filings for its Hong Kong initial public offering that the investigation could result in significant fines. Reuters did not detail how the $100 million would be distributed or what changes Shein would be required to make.
RELATED STORIES: Walmart to Pay Drivers $100 Million in Settlement Over Misleading Pay | Amazon to Pay $8.25 Million in Delivery Lawsuit Settlement
So many complaints
The complaints include reports submitted to both the FTC and the Better Business Bureau. They raised questions about missing orders and how Shein handled customers who disputed delivery records.
The complaint totals also cover several years and include issues beyond shipping , so they should not be read as a count of confirmed delivery failures.
Along with its own clothing, Shein sells products from outside merchants through its online marketplace. Those listings include toys, household appliances, and home decor.
The FTC means business
The FTC has previously pursued online retailers over shipping delays and refunds. Its Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule requires sellers to have a reasonable basis for advertised shipping times. When no time is stated, sellers generally must ship within 30 days.
If a seller cannot ship on time, it must let customers choose to agree to a delay or cancel for a refund. The FTC says gift cards and store credit do not qualify as refunds for merchandise that was never shipped.
Those requirements provide context for the agency’s work on delivery complaints, although Reuters’ report did not identify the specific provisions underlying the Shein settlement.
In 2020, Fashion Nova agreed to a $9.3 million settlement after the FTC alleged it failed to meet shipping promises and improperly issued gift cards instead of refunds. In 2023, Hey Dude agreed to pay $1.95 million to settle allegations involving shipping delays, refunds and the suppression of negative reviews.

UPS will raise daily shipping rates for Ground, Air , and International services by an average net 5.9% beginning Dec. 21, 2026. The increase takes effect four days before Christmas and will carry into 2027.
What’s Related
The carrier will also change the ZIP codes subject to area surcharges and the shipping zones assigned to certain ZIP codes. The minimum billable weight for packages requiring additional handling will rise from 40 pounds to 50 pounds.
Individual customers’ increases will depend on what they ship and the terms of their UPS agreements. The carrier has not yet released the detailed rate previews needed to calculate how prices for specific shipments will change.
Daily rates apply to customers with scheduled UPS pickups or contracts that provide those rates. Customers using UPS’s Small Business Rates program face a separate increase, also beginning Dec. 21.
RELATED STORIES: UPS to Hire 100,000 Seasonal Workers for Holiday Rush | UPS Rolls Out New AI Tools for Tracking, Returns and Customer Service
Other changes
The higher minimum billable weight could increase charges for affected packages even when their actual weight stays the same. It raises the minimum weight UPS uses to calculate shipping charges for a qualifying package.
For example, a qualifying package billed at the 40-pound minimum would now be billed at 50 pounds, unless its actual or dimensional weight is higher. That change is separate from the shipping rate increase.
The ZIP code changes could also affect costs. Area surcharges add fees for designated locations, while shipping zones help determine shipment prices based on origin and destination.
UPS is also changing its fuel surcharge tables for domestic Ground, Ground Saver, and Domestic Air shipments beginning Nov. 2. Those changes take effect seven weeks before the annual rate increase.
New surge fees are coming
UPS plans an additional per-package surge fee for certain customers sending domestic Ground and Ground Saver shipments from specified origin ZIP codes. The fee will take effect on or after Dec. 21.
The carrier expects to release details in early November, including the affected origin ZIP codes. Its current notice does not specify the fee amount or fully explain which customers will qualify.
Those charges add another variable to shipping budgets. The average rate increase alone will not show how much a customer’s total bill will rise.
Small businesses face separate pricing
UPS will raise its published Small Business Rates for Ground, Air, and International services by 4.5% on Dec. 21. A 5% domestic and international fuel surcharge will also apply to those rates.
Customers in that program will face the same increase in the minimum billable weight for additional-handling packages, from 40 pounds to 50 pounds.
The daily-rate increase matches FedEx ’s announced average increase of 5.9%, although FedEx’s change takes effect Jan. 4, 2027, two weeks after UPS.
Comparing the carriers’ prices for specific shipments will require more information from UPS. “More detailed rate previews will be available at a later date,” the carrier said.

Supply chain teams want AI tools to help them make better decisions, but moving from a demo to daily use takes more than technology . In this Q&A, we asked Brent Hasenkamp , SVP of Sales for North America at o9 Solutions , about what holds companies back, how AI can help with excess inventory , and how planning tools can inform tariff decisions.
What’s Related
Supply Chain 24/7: What is holding companies back from getting more out of AI?
Brent Hasenkamp: I think the learnings have been, yes, you can do something quickly, but do you actually have the governance? Do you have the constraints? Do you have the context? And do you really have the skills to make it repeatable, consistent, and something that can actually be governed inside of an organization?
We’re seeing that companies that start with a clear statement, then put AI into practice with knowledge agents or tools that can analyze performance after the fact, are able to build on those initial applications.

SC247: How do you see AI changing the work people do?
Hasenkamp : I think whenever we get into a technological revolution, much like we had with the wave of the internet and cloud and what that looks like for business , companies realize they must transform. They have to reimagine roles and understand how they are able to accomplish more than they ever could before.
At so many of our client organizations where we’re infusing these AI capabilities, the ultimate goal isn’t massive headcount reduction; it’s to say, how do I spot, detect, and act on things I never would have been able to see earlier. And then ultimately, how am I building more equipped knowledge workers?
Brent Hasenkamp
“The ultimate goal isn’t massive headcount reduction; it’s to say, how do I spot, detect, and act on things I never would have been able to see earlier.”
SC247: Can you give an example of how AI helps with excess inventory?
Hasenkamp : As an example, if the product is valuable enough, and it makes sense, can I move that to a pocket of demand where there is movement? So that’s one decision AI can help with: rebalancing.
Another one can be around excess inventory: Do I have anything else coming in? How can I slow it down or stop it altogether because I don’t need it? So that’s a second example.
The third one is if I truly can’t move the excess inventory and I don’t have great ideas to create demand, I can send it to my engineering team and can we understand what we can actually use this product for.
SC247: What common planning problems do you see?
Hasenkamp : I think the organizations that have both the biggest opportunity but also some of the biggest challenges are the ones that have never really had planning in any sort of systematic way before. They’ve largely operated in offline Excel sheets and relied on a lot of tribal knowledge to plan.
SC247: How are companies using planning tools to respond to tariffs?
Hasenkamp : They’re bringing in revenue, bringing in COGS, and doing all of this work. They were able to use the o9 platform in less than two business days to say, ultimately, here is my exposure, here’s a number of different scenarios because it was also wildly uncertain. And here are the decisions that we would either need to make from a sourcing perspective, or if we don’t change anything, here is the gross margin impact, and here’s the pricing uplift that we would have to have to protect our margin.
Brent Hasenkamp is SVP of Sales for North America at o9 Solutions .

context_references.quote: Nearly all food and drink businesses surveyed identified serious labor rights violations in their supply chains during the past year, according to research commissioned by the British Standards Institution (BSI) and the Chartered Institute of Procurement & Supply (CIPS).

source_document.body:
Nearly all food and drink businesses surveyed identified serious labor rights violations in their supply chains during the past year, according to research commissioned by the British Standards Institution (BSI) and the Chartered Institute of Procurement & Supply (CIPS). At 97%, food and beverage respondents reported the highest rate of any industry surveyed.
What’s Related
The findings also point to weaknesses in how businesses track their response. Only 36% of food and drink firms could demonstrate the impact of whistleblowing and other channels for reporting concerns, the lowest among the industries studied.
Meanwhile, 39% did not require suppliers to identify their own suppliers in contracts. That leaves companies with less information about the businesses and workers involved further down their supply chains.
Together, the findings show that identifying labor problems and demonstrating improvements for workers remain separate challenges. The 97% figure covers several types of violations and should not be read as a finding that every affected company discovered forced labor.
RELATED: $2.03 an Hour: Labor Dept. Finds Major Wage Violations at Warehouse
Too many unanswered questions
The research found a gap between what business leaders believe they can prove and how much of their supply chains they can actually see. Across industries, 80% said they had enough evidence to demonstrate that their supply chains were free from violations, while only 22% reported comprehensive visibility of third-party suppliers.
For food and drink companies, the lack of supplier disclosure requirements adds another obstacle. Knowing a direct supplier does not necessarily mean knowing which businesses provide its ingredients, materials, or services, or what conditions workers face at those businesses.
“The challenge is then being able to demonstrate impact and show that these interventions are improving outcomes for workers. Addressing modern slavery risk is about driving meaningful change,” said Harold Pradal, president of assurance services at BSI.
What happens after a violation is found?
The research also examined how companies respond when they uncover problems. BSI’s U.S. announcement said 53% worked with suppliers to address violations rather than immediately ending contracts, while 11% described their response as limited.
However, continuing a supplier relationship does not, by itself, show that working conditions have improved. The food and beverage findings raise a similar question about reporting channels: businesses may have ways for workers to raise concerns without being able to show what changed afterward.
“The challenge is no longer whether businesses are taking action, but whether they can demonstrate that their action is driving real improvements for vulnerable workers,” Pradal said.

BMW’s next electric SUV won’t just be bigger. The iX7 will sit at the top of the brand’s EV lineup when it debuts in 2027, bringing a more luxurious option to the mix.
BMW moves upscale with the iX7, its first luxury 3-row EV
After the new X5 and iX5, the X7, BMW’s biggest SUV, is due for a Neue Klasse overhaul. BMW said the second-generation X7 will arrive in 2027, including the first fully electric version, the iX7.
Ahead of its upcoming debut, camouflaged prototypes have been spotted testing , revealing a few design changes.
Although it won’t fully adopt BMW’s Neue Klasse design, like the iX3, the three-row SUV appears to feature a slimmer, more upright Kidney Grille instead of the traditional wide BMW Grille.

The iX7 also swaps conventional pull-style door handles for small handles on the vehicle’s pillar. It also retains split headlights rather than the updated Neue Klasse-style headlights on the iX3 (shown below on the right).
While BMW has yet to reveal details, a Reddit user who claims to work at BMW’s factory in South Carolina and has seen the second-generation X7 shared a few new details.
Like the X5 and iX5, the new X7 and iX7 will retain a more traditional design rather than going full-on Neue Klasse, including the Kidney Grille. The user also said BMW is dropping the split tailgate, which it did with the new X5, in favor of a standard one-piece tailgate.
Inside, the dashboard and center console are similar to the new X5, but with upgraded tech and features from the new 7 Series sedan.
BMW said the new 7 Series sedan “takes the lead when it comes to the introduction of technologies from the Neue Klasse into existing models.”
Optional features will reportedly include the upgraded 31.3″ 8K BMW Theatre Screen for rear passengers and a 14.6″ BMW Passenger Screen. It will also have optional touch screen panels on the rear doors, the user said.
While most of the claims make sense, we’ll have to wait for BMW to confirm it officially. The new X7 and iX7 are expected to debut in mid-2027.
Like the iX5 60 xDrive, the three-row iX7 is expected to use a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain. The iX5’s AWD setup delivers a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque, enabling it to hit 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds.
BMW iX5 60 xDrive hits 460 kW (Source: BMW)
The iX5 uses a massive 144 kWh battery, which BMW said offers up to 435 miles of range. It will also use an 800V electrical system for fast charging.
BMW showed just how fast it can charge during a media event in Southern California earlier this month, where the iX5 60 xDrive hit a peak of 464 kW. With up to 460 kW peak charging, the iX5 60 xDrive can add up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes, BMW says.
The new X7 and iX7 are expected to go into production at BMW’s Spartanburg plant in SC in late 2027, joining the new iX5.

context_references.quote: Diesel has separated from both gasoline and crude oil and set records on the strength of lost global refining capacity, a Russian export pullback, and policy and geography that most fuel buyers never see, which means the mental model of watching oil prices to predict diesel no longer works and the fuel surcharge pegged to a lagging weekly average no longer fully protects a carrier’s margin.

source_document.body:
For the better part of eight months the price of diesel has climbed to levels that gasoline has not come close to matching, and for a carrier whose single largest variable cost is the fuel in the tank, that split is not a curiosity but a direct hit to the bottom line, which is why a recent F3 conversation with Patrick De Haan, the GasBuddy analyst who has tracked pump prices since 2009, is worth carriers understanding in full, because the force driving diesel to records has far less to do with the price of oil than almost anyone at the counter assumes.
De Haan, whose firm tracks gasoline and diesel at roughly 150,000 stations across the United States and Canada and has been helping motorists find lower prices for 26 years, called this the single most volatile stretch he has seen, and not because of one dramatic spike. Volatility normally arrives with a hurricane or a geopolitical flare-up and fades in a week or two. This has run since March, cooling in June and July, roaring back in August and September, and never really settling. What makes it different from the last big run-up, though, is that diesel and gasoline have completely decoupled, and the reasons expose how little the fuel most truckers buy actually tracks the headlines about crude.
average gasoline and diesel prices stubbornly holding in familiar territory: $4.26/gal for gasoline, $6.35/gal for diesel. prices may slip a few cents but long term relief remains elusive. — Patrick De Haan (@GasBuddyGuy) October 27, 2026
A Record For Diesel, Not For Gas
The numbers tell the story of the divergence. De Haan noted that diesel blew past its 2022 record of 5.81 dollars a gallon, touched around 6.50 a few weeks before the event, and had eased only slightly to about 6.35. Gasoline, by contrast, remains roughly 70 cents below its own 2022 high. In the last comparable episode, the post-pandemic inflation of 2022, gasoline and diesel both set records together and moved more or less in tandem. This time the two fuels have pulled apart so sharply that Americans are discovering in real time something they rarely have to think about, which is that gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and crude oil are different products with different economics, and that a barrel of oil is close to worthless until a refinery turns it into something usable.
That last point is the hinge of De Haan’s entire explanation. Everyone watches the price of crude, but crude you cannot refine does you no good, and the real story of the past year is a loss of refining capacity rather than a shortage of oil in the ground.
Why Refining Is The Whole Game
Not all crude is alike, and that is where diesel gets squeezed. De Haan compared it to the oil aisle at an auto parts store, where there is no single weight or grade. Refineries run different blends, from the light grades to the heavier crude that Canada, Venezuela, Iran, and Russia tend to produce, and heavier input yields more heavy product such as diesel. That matters because the countries sitting at the center of this year’s disruptions are heavy-crude players. De Haan put Iran at roughly 55 percent heavy production, noted the year’s long debate over hard-to-refine Venezuelan barrels, and stressed that a refinery generally cannot simply swap one type of crude for another. When the heavy barrels or the plants that process them come under pressure, diesel feels it first.
The structural backdrop makes the squeeze worse. Diesel has run above gasoline for about two decades, a gap that widened after the ultra-low-sulfur diesel specification took hold around 2006. And the United States is no longer the world’s largest refiner, having been overtaken by China in the last year. De Haan flagged China as an underappreciated wild card, because it has throttled some of its refining output to protect its own crude access and strategic reserves, pulling capacity out of a global market that is already short.
The Russia And Ukraine Shock
Layered on top of those slow-moving forces is a fast one. De Haan traced the exponential jump in diesel since July to Russia pulling back on diesel exports, a serious problem given that Russia produces about 10 percent of the world’s diesel. The cause is the Ukrainian drone campaign against Russian refineries, which began last October but has grown far more effective as drone technology advanced over the past year, degrading Russia’s refining sector to the point of domestic fuel rationing and leaving less supply to export. Earlier in the year the Strait of Hormuz and tensions involving Iran were already lifting crude, so the market now carries both pressures at once, a crude-price factor and a refining-capacity factor stacked together. The oil disruption moves the base price, but the refining losses are what sent diesel specifically into record territory.
How The Pump Price Actually Gets Built
De Haan then walked the chain from the trading screen to the truck stop, and the mechanics explain why two carriers hundreds of miles apart can pay wildly different prices on the same day. The foundation for diesel across North America is the NYMEX ultra-low-sulfur diesel contract, essentially a delivered New York Harbor price for diesel on a barge with no taxes attached. From that foundation, regional refining balances take over, and the spread between markets can run 40 to 60 cents a gallon depending on whether you are fueling in New York, Michigan, Florida, Texas, or California.
Geography and infrastructure drive those gaps. The Colonial Pipeline, which De Haan likened to an aorta running in a crescent from the Houston area up through the mid-Atlantic to New York, means wholesale markets along its path price off the Gulf Coast. The Gulf Coast holds the most refining capacity in the country and is usually one of the cheapest places to buy fuel, which is why parts of the lower and mid-Atlantic that tap directly into that pipeline can be surprisingly cheap. But that same export-capable coast can swing to a premium when Europe is scrambling for diesel it can no longer get from Russia. The West Coast runs expensive because California policy has narrowed refining capacity and taxes are high, and even the Great Lakes saw diesel jump recently on localized refining trouble, since those plants lean on Western Canadian crude.
The Volatility Carriers Feel, And The Surcharge That Lags It
The piece most relevant to a trucking operation is how fast wholesale prices now move. The wholesale level, known in the industry as the rack, historically reset once at the end of the day, around five or six o’clock. In this market De Haan said there have been stretches, particularly March and April, when the rack moved intraday, and the difference between filling a tank truck at 5:55 and 6:05 could be 50, 60, 70, even 80 cents a gallon at wholesale. That gets passed down the chain unevenly, because retail stations tend to lag by one to three days on the way up and stay sticky on the way down, and their underground tanks turn over faster than most people think, on average every two to four days and far more often at high-volume truck stops. The idea that a station is selling fuel it priced ten days ago is simply wrong.
This is exactly where the fuel surcharge mechanism strains. Most surcharge programs are pegged to the Department of Energy’s weekly national average on-highway diesel price, a single number published once a week. In a market where the rack can swing most of a dollar in ten minutes and regional spreads run half a dollar or more, a weekly national average cannot keep pace. A carrier running the expensive lanes De Haan described, the West Coast, the Great Lakes during a refining hiccup, or a Gulf Coast gone to export premium, can be paying well above the index that sets the surcharge, and because the index lags the spike and the recovery arrives slowly, the gap between what a truck pays at the island and what the surcharge gives back is real money that comes straight out of margin . The lesson is not to ignore the surcharge but to know that in a decoupled, refining-driven market it recovers less of the true cost than it did when fuels moved together.
What It Means Going Forward
De Haan was measured about blame. Oil companies, he argued, are price takers rather than price makers, and the proof is that back in January and February, before any of this broke, crude sat at 50 to 60 dollars a barrel and producers were not thriving. Convenience stores, where retail margins have run unusually high lately, are riding the same volatility and increasingly make their money on everything other than fuel. The uncomfortable macro note he left on was that the forecasts heading into 2026 had widely predicted a glut of crude, and that expectation ended abruptly on March 1, with no quick return to a calm, well-supplied market in sight. For carriers, the takeaway is that diesel is now driven by a different and more fragile set of levers than the oil price everyone watches, and planning fuel cost around the headline price of crude is planning around the wrong number.
Why It Matters
Diesel has separated from both gasoline and crude oil and set records on the strength of lost global refining capacity, a Russian export pullback, and policy and geography that most fuel buyers never see, which means the mental model of watching oil prices to predict diesel no longer works and the fuel surcharge pegged to a lagging weekly average no longer fully protects a carrier’s margin. For anyone whose costs live and die with the pump, the move is to track diesel on its own terms, understand the regional and refining forces actually setting the price, and treat the gap between real fuel cost and surcharge recovery as a number to manage rather than assume away.
This article is based on an F3 conversation with Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. Price figures, dates, and market characterizations are as presented by the speaker at the event. Fuel surcharge mechanics reflect standard industry practice tied to the U.S. Department of Energy weekly diesel price index.

China Gold suspended open-pit mining after slope instability on May 22. ( Image: China Gold International. )
Posted By: Mining.com Staff October 27, 2026
China Gold International Resources (TSX: CGG; HKEX: 2099) has resumed open-pit mining at its Chang Shan Hao (CSH) gold mine in Inner Mongolia after a slope instability halted mining for about four and a half months.
Mining restarted in early October following remediation work and regulatory filings, the company said in a release on Monday . The processing plant continued to treat low-grade stockpiled ore during the suspension, and the company maintained its 2026 production forecast of about 70,700 to 83,600 oz., compared with 96,816 oz. in 2025.
CSH produced 42,854 oz. of gold in the first half of the year, including about five weeks after mining stopped, according to the company’s interim results . It needed about 27,900 oz. in the second half to reach the low end of its annual forecast. The company didn’t provide third-quarter output figures in Monday’s release.
China Gold suspended open-pit mining after the localized slope instability on May 22. No casualties or equipment losses were reported.
The company hired geotechnical experts to assess the slope and develop remediation plans. By the end of September, it had completed the key interim work needed to restart mining, including restoring mine roads, removing loose material and hazardous rock, reinforcing the affected slope and installing drainage systems.
Hazards addressed
A third-party organization evaluated the work and found that the hazards affecting mining had been addressed, the company said. Mining resumed after China Gold completed a filing process with emergency management authorities.
China Gold, which uses heap leaching at CSH, plans to blend freshly mined ore with stockpiled material and says it will continue monitoring conditions and subsequent engineering work at the mine.
The open pit was approaching the end of its mine life, with slope stability becoming a more prominent factor in planning as the pit deepened, China Gold said in its 2025 annual results .
China Gold also operates the Jiama copper-gold mine in Tibet, which produced 70,883 tonnes of copper and 80,409 oz. of gold in 2025.
Another TSX-listed miner operating in China, Silvercorp Metals (TSX: SVM; NYSE-A: SVM), has suspended mining at its GC silver-lead-zinc mine in Guangdong province since late June. The company says it must update the mine’s development plan and complete safety upgrades before production can resume, which it expects in November 2027.
Shares in China Gold International were up 3% to $33.22 apiece Tuesday afternoon in Toronto, valuing the company at $13 billion (US$9.2 billion).

When it comes to Mopars from the golden era, there's no shortage of them on the classic car market. Whether we're talking about mundane examples or rare muscle cars, there are plenty to choose from. However, most of these vehicles are still rotting away in junkyards .
Mopar City of Oregon, Illinois, is one of those places. It's home to over a thousand vehicles, including anything from A-body and E-body compacts to B-body intermediates and C-body full-size rigs. The yard was recently documented by Ryan Brutt of YouTube's "Auto Archaeology," with several videos posted online.
Ryan's latest vlog shows a large portion of the yard that's loaded with B-body Mopars. This platform underpinned Chrysler mid-size vehicles from 1962 to 1979, and it's obviously famous for being used in iconic Dodge and Plymouth muscle cars. It's arguably one of the most interesting areas of Mopar City.
Of course, this section includes quite a few mundane vehicles. The B-body platform also underpinned bread-and-butter nameplates like the Dodge Coronet and Plymouth Belvedere . These sold like hot cakes in four-door body styles, and they're quite common in junkyards. Moreover, many two-door coupes are also pretty common.
The Dodge Charger is one of the best examples out there. Dodge delivered over 370,000 units from 1966 to 1971, with most of them equipped with small-block V8 engines. While the R/T version is indeed somewhat rare, the base Charger is a common junkyard find. And this one is loaded with them.
The Plymouth Road Runner was also a strong seller, and you'll see quite a few in the video below. Naturally, they're all 383-cubic-inch (6.3-liter) V8 cars, so no rare Hemi or Six-Barrel vehicles. But Ryan also found a few cars that are actually rare.
One of them is a 1970 Dodge Charger of the R/T variety. They're not exactly rare by overall production numbers, as Dodge delivered about 10,000 units, but this one was born with a 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) Six-Pack V8 . The 390-horsepower mill found its way into only 684 cars that year. Ryan says it's an automatic car, which makes it one of 337 examples fitted with this drivetrain combo.
Things get even more interesting if we also factor in the EW1 white exterior. The 1970 Charger Registry states that only 4.3% of all R/Ts were ordered in this color. It's unclear exactly how many were Six-Pack vehicles, but we're probably looking at fewer than 15 units made with this drivetrain setup.
The second vehicle that caught my attention is the 1970 Plymouth Belvedere that pops up at the 1:07-minute mark. Yes, the Belvedere was Plymouth's entry-level B-body, and it was built in large numbers, but things are a bit different for this 1970 iteration.
For starters, 1970 was the final year for the nameplate , and Plymouth didn't sell that many. Records show that only 24,246 examples rolled off the assembly line. That's a notable drop from 1966, when Plymouth sold nearly 190,000 units. More importantly, this Belvedere is a two-door coupe, which is the rarest body style when it comes to the 1970 version. Specifically, only 4,717 units were ordered like this.
But here's what makes this Belvedere stand out: it appears to be a painted top car. What's that? Well, it was a more affordable way of getting a two-tone appearance compared to the vinyl top. The roof was often finished in a contrasting color; in this case, it's white over B5 Blue. And it's a very rare option on B-body vehicles.
How do we know it's a true two-tone car and not a vinyl-top model that was repainted? Well, this Belvedere would need to have a V02 code on the fender tag. But Ryan doesn't lift the hood, so it remains a mystery. However, it does look like the vehicle still has the original paint, and there are no signs of a vinyl roof.
There are no records as to how many 1970 Belvederes were ordered with this option, but experts agree that only 1% to 3% of the cars were sold with the two-tone feature. That's anywhere between 47 and 142 coupes. Enough to make this Belvedere worth saving. Unlike the Charger R/T Six-Pack , which is just a shell. Check them out in the video below.

Merchants Fleet has expanded FleetShare , its managed vehicle access program, to Puerto Rico, the company said on Oct. 20 . The operation went live Sept. 14 with 113 Merchants-managed vehicles supporting an unnamed global e-commerce company’s last-mile delivery operations on the island.
It is FleetShare’s first deployment outside the continental United States. Drivers at the site reserve and access vehicles through a mobile app, according to the release.
FleetShare now covers more than 8,000 managed vehicles across North America. Merchants, which leases vehicles to package delivery companies , runs the program for last-mile delivery, utility, and other fleets that share vehicles among drivers.
“Our expansion into Puerto Rico is more than geographic growth,” said Whitney Reynolds, vice president of FleetShare at Merchants Fleet. “It demonstrates FleetShare’s flexibility and reinforces our vision of helping organizations rethink how they manage fleet operations.”
How drivers get vehicles under FleetShare
FleetShare is designed to get a driver into a vehicle without a manual key handoff, whiteboard, spreadsheet, or phone call, the release said. It pairs connected key boxes with driver profiles and reservation and assignment tools. Fleet managers track assignments, availability, and utilization in one place.
The key boxes run on cellular service and can be installed wherever there is power and a connection, according to Merchants’ product page . The release said the system operates independently of a customer’s Wi-Fi or local network.
In October 2025, Merchants added three features to FleetShare, Work Truck reported : keyless access through automaker and third-party integrations, geofencing, and end-of-use driver surveys.
Customer and contract terms not disclosed
But the release does not name the customer or disclose contract terms or pricing. Nor does it say what types of vehicles make up the Puerto Rico fleet, how they are serviced on the island, or whether more will be added.
For now, the 113 vehicles are the only measure of the deal’s size. Reynolds said the program is built for fleets of any size.
“Whether a customer is operating dozens of vehicles or thousands across multiple locations, FleetShare helps simplify fleet management,” she said.
Why it matters: FleetShare’s Puerto Rico launch puts app-based vehicle access into a 113-vehicle last-mile operation, the program’s first outside the continental U.S. The customer, contract terms, and how the island fleet is serviced remain undisclosed.

Recent freight fraud investigations have exposed millions of dollars in cargo losses across the United States. Federal prosecutors recently charged a driver in an alleged $12 million cargo theft conspiracy involving established trucking companies. A California trucking owner pleaded guilty in a separate $2.1 million identity theft case. Another investigation uncovered a nationwide cargo theft ring that purchased existing motor carriers to secure freight.
Although these investigations involve different suspects, several reveal the same vulnerability within freight transportation. Criminals exploit legitimate business identities, established operating authorities, and trusted communications to gain control of shipments. Their tactics can make fraudulent transactions appear legitimate during routine carrier verification. The question is whether employees know what to verify before releasing freight.
Established authority does not establish identity
Federal prosecutors recently charged Nursulton Khaydarov in connection with an alleged cargo theft conspiracy exceeding $12 million. Investigators identified at least 24 shipments involving trucking companies that suspects allegedly purchased or controlled. The operation relied on established carrier identities to obtain legitimate freight assignments. Khaydarov pleaded not guilty in federal court in Bridgeport, Connecticut.
A separate Chicago-area fraud case involved more than $10 million in stolen copper and liquor. Investigators described suspects using multiple identities to impersonate legitimate transportation businesses. Those representations helped the operation obtain access to valuable shipments. The deception centered on convincing victims they were dealing with authorized transportation providers.
In New Jersey, a fake freight broker redirected a $273,000 seafood shipment . The driver followed fraudulent delivery instructions that diverted the truck from its intended destination. Authorities discovered the shipment at a North Arlington location before the cargo disappeared. The incident demonstrated how unauthorized instructions can compromise a legitimate shipment already in transit.
These cases expose an important distinction between operating authority and actual control. A valid motor carrier number does not establish who currently controls the business. Legitimate paperwork cannot independently confirm the identity of someone issuing transportation instructions. That distinction matters whenever employees assign, release, or redirect freight.
What verification needs to catch
The Certified Fraud Compliance Officer (CFCO) course addresses these vulnerabilities through structured fraud prevention education. FreightWaves developed the training around a repeatable five-layer verification process for transportation professionals. The process examines Company, Person, Insurance, Activity, and Shipment Fit before employees authorize freight movement. Each layer addresses information that criminals may exploit to make fraudulent transactions appear legitimate.
Consider a trucking company with several years of operating history and an active motor carrier authority. Those records may appear legitimate even after an ownership or contact change. An employee who checks only registration status could overlook the person actually controlling the transaction. Additional identity and activity verification can help expose inconsistencies before someone receives freight.
The training also addresses double brokering, carrier impersonation, communication takeovers, and manipulated insurance documentation. These schemes exploit different weaknesses throughout the transportation process. Employees must recognize suspicious changes and understand when additional verification becomes necessary. More importantly, they need clear procedures for stopping a transaction when information does not match.
Technology cannot make every decision
Carrier monitoring platforms provide valuable information about authority, insurance, operating history, and potential fraud indicators. However, an active authority alone cannot establish who currently controls a transportation company. Digital records also cannot independently confirm every person who arrives at a shipping facility. Employees still need procedures for resolving discrepancies between available information and actual shipment activity.
An unexpected contact change, unfamiliar dispatch instructions, or conflicting driver information may warrant additional scrutiny. These circumstances do not automatically establish criminal activity, but they require verification before freight moves. That responsibility extends beyond the brokerage office to dispatchers, drivers, and warehouse personnel. Every transfer of control creates another opportunity to confirm who is handling the shipment.
Fraud prevention requires more than identifying suspicious activity after a loss. Employees need to understand what to question, how to verify information, and when to escalate concerns. Technology can support those decisions, but it cannot replace consistent procedures. Confidence comes from verification, not assumptions.
Why It Matters
Recent investigations show how criminals exploit legitimate transportation identities to gain control of freight. Training employees to recognize those tactics and verify information can help stop fraudulent transactions before shipments disappear.

U.S. online grocery sales rose 20.7% in the third quarter of 2026, accounting for a record 20.9% of total grocery spending, according to new research from Brick Meets Click. Delivery generated three-quarters of the increase, growing much faster than pickup.
What’s Related
The findings draw on the firm’s monthly grocery shopper surveys for July, August and September. Online grocery sales have now grown more than 20% year over year for eight consecutive quarters.
More households bought groceries online, and existing customers placed orders more often. The quarterly base of monthly buyers reached almost 62% of U.S. households, up 1.2 percentage points from a year earlier, while order frequency increased nearly 14%.
September set a separate record, with nearly 64% of households buying groceries online that month. Online grocery’s rising share of spending came as in-store grocery sales declined compared with the third quarter of 2025.
Delivery grows faster than pickup
All three ways of receiving online grocery orders posted sales gains, but delivery accounted for most of the growth. Its sales rose more than 30% from a year earlier, adding more than five percentage points to its share of online grocery spending.
Pickup sales grew in the mid-single digits. Ship-to-home sales also rose, though by less than the overall market’s 20.7% gain.
The survey distinguishes delivery from parcel shipping . Delivery includes orders brought by a retailer ’s employees or services such as Instacart and Shipt, while ship-to-home covers orders arriving through carriers and couriers such as FedEx , UPS , and USPS . Pickup includes orders collected inside or outside a store or at a designated location or locker.
“Many of the newer eGrocery offerings focus on shorter order cycle times, while others strive to provide ways to avoid paying more than necessary,” said David Bishop, a partner at Brick Meets Click.
Shoppers use different services
Customers increasingly used several ways to receive their groceries within the same month. During the quarter, 17% of monthly online grocery buyers used delivery, pickup and ship-to-home, up more than five percentage points from a year earlier.
That overlap coincided with a rise in ordering frequency. By the end of the quarter, 81% of U.S. households had purchased groceries online at least once.
Shoppers’ stated likelihood of using the same delivery or pickup service again within 30 days reached 62%. That compares with 61% in 2025 and 56% in 2024.

source_document.body:
JACKSONVILLE, Florida — Knight-Swift Transportation has reduced its approved brokerage carrier pool by approximately 70% over the past two years as the trucking giant tightens carrier vetting standards amid growing concerns over cargo theft , highway safety and potential broker liability .
CEO Adam Miller disclosed the reduction Tuesday during his keynote address at the second annual WEX OTR Summit in Jacksonville, Florida, saying the company has become increasingly selective about which motor carriers it allows to transport freight through its brokerage operations.
“We’re down 70% from maybe two years ago,” Miller told attendees. “Because we really vetted the type of carrier that we want.”
Knight-Swift sees opportunity for more durable freight recovery
Miller’s remarks come as Knight-Swift reports improving truckload market conditions despite relatively weak freight demand.
During his keynote, he said available trucking capacity continues to tighten while national tender rejection rates remain elevated.
Miller said stricter federal enforcement and more selective broker-carrier relationships could prevent another rapid influx of trucking capacity during the next freight market upcycle.
He said that those changes could help create a more sustainable recovery rather than the sharp increases and declines in trucking rates experienced in recent years.
The second annual WEX OTR Summit drew more than 115 attendees, including trucking executives, fuel providers, technology companies and other transportation industry representatives.
Miller said Knight-Swift’s brokerage business has strengthened its carrier qualification requirements over the past three years, partly in response to increasingly sophisticated cargo theft schemes.
“Cargo theft went from a couple bad actors to organized crime,” Miller said.
The company requires motor carriers to have been operating for at least one year before they can participate in its brokerage network, according to Miller.
“We wouldn’t allow a carrier to come into our business unless they’ve been active for a year,” he said.
Miller said some large freight brokers have historically allowed newly registered trucking companies to access freight with minimal operating history, creating potential exposure to fraud, cargo theft and safety-related claims.
He said that requiring carriers to establish a longer operating history could help brokers identify potential risks before tendering loads.
Broker liability adds pressure to carrier vetting
Miller said recent developments involving broker liability could accelerate changes in how freight brokers evaluate motor carriers.
He referenced the U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II , arguing that brokers could face greater legal exposure when they hire trucking companies with questionable safety records.
“Now you have brokers who have some skin in the game if they’re negligent in the carrier that they hire to move the load,” Miller said.
He suggested that some brokers have historically prioritized lower transportation costs over more stringent carrier qualification requirements.
Miller said potential legal exposure could prompt brokers to more closely examine carrier safety records, operating history and insurance coverage.
“If you’re going to be willing to put in, to engage with a carrier that has an unsafe CSA score that’s over threshold, you’re at risk,” he said.
CSA refers to the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration ’s Compliance, Safety, Accountability program, which uses inspection, crash and investigation data to identify potential motor carrier safety concerns.
Miller said that CSA scores do not necessarily provide a definitive measure of a carrier’s safety performance but said unfavorable scores could become a significant factor in litigation.
He warned that stricter carrier screening could substantially reduce the number of trucking companies eligible to haul brokered freight.
“When we start dialing in these different criteria you should be using to vet your carriers, the carrier pool you can work with is going to be significantly smaller,” Miller said.
Cargo theft, insurance costs create additional challenges
Miller said the growth of organized cargo theft has forced Knight-Swift to reconsider the risks associated with hiring unfamiliar carriers.
The company uses outside carriers in its brokerage operations, including power-only arrangements in which a contracted motor carrier supplies a tractor to haul a trailer.
Miller said those arrangements make carrier screening particularly important.
The CEO also warned that major trucking accident verdicts and potential broker liability could increase insurance costs for freight brokers.
He suggested insurers may reassess their exposure to claims involving motor carriers hired by brokers and could charge higher premiums to account for that risk.
“Brokers are gonna have to pay multiples of what they’re paying now to keep the same insurance limits,” Miller said.
Miller said shippers are also becoming concerned about whether they could face litigation if a motor carrier’s insurance coverage is insufficient to satisfy a large accident judgment.
“A lot of concern, a lot of discussions with customers around this topic,” he said.
Smaller carriers could face tougher access to freight
Miller said more restrictive broker qualification standards could make it harder for newly established trucking companies to obtain loads, particularly those relying heavily on the spot freight market.
He suggested the changes could reinforce a broader tightening of trucking capacity already underway because of increased federal enforcement of commercial driver’s license requirements and other safety regulations.
Miller said the trucking industry has historically experienced rapid increases in capacity during strong freight markets, followed by steep declines in freight rates when too many carriers enter the market.
More stringent broker screening could create an additional barrier to entry, he said.
“That’s going to eliminate probably the cheapest capacity, the less compliant carriers out there in the market,” Miller said.
Why it matters: Knight-Swift CEO Adam Mille says a supply-driven recovery could lead to higher transportation rates and longer-lasting capacity constraints even without a significant rebound in freight volumes in 2027.
