The changes made back then are fresh enough to still be relevant, but, for one reason or another, the company decided to update the bike again – making it in the process the most accessible, most advanced and most versatile large-capacity bike of this kind ever made by Triumph.
Triumph's changes target everything, from the mechanical bits that influence the performance numbers to the way the bike behaves and handles on the road, with all these upgrades topped off by a visual refresh.
I'll start, as usual, with the bike's frame, which remains the same tubular steel frame configuration as before, fitted with aluminum outriggers, a subframe, and a swingarm made of the same material.
The suspension system that ties into the frame is described by Triumph as the most sophisticated semi-active setup the company has ever used on any of its products. Responsible for that bold description is the Showa Eera Heightflex self-lowering suspension system.
Born into the world some eight years ago, the tech comes with three damping settings, and, on top of that, it can automatically lower the seat by 30 mm when the bike stops, and can make life easier for riders when the bike needs to be fitted on a center stand.
Photo: Triumph The suspension system, which consists of 49 mm forks and a monoshock, supports wheels sized 19 inches at the front and 17 inches at the rear, which move under the power supplied by the mighty 1200 triple engine (1,160cc) and the six-speed transmission that controls it.
The powerplant has been at the receiving end of some serious upgrades that targeted the cylinder heads, pistons, inlet and exhaust valves (the larger exhaust tech is a stainless steel 3-into-1 header system), and fuel injection. The changes made to these parts led to the engine now developing eight horsepower more than before, for a total of 156 hp at 9,250 rpm.
Torque levels for the new Tiger 1200 stand at 130 Nm at 6,750 rpm, and there are up to eight ride modes the bike can be set in: Road, Rain, Eco, Sport, Off-road, Off-road Pro, and two configurable ones.
The new Tiger 1200 brings along, as another novelty, front and rear Bosch radar, which works in conjunction with cornering ABS, traction control, and the six-axis IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit).
Photo: Triumph The revised and improved engine goes hand in hand with updates the Brits performed to the way the bike interacts and connects to the rider. More specifically, Triumph went for a new seven-inch touchscreen that runs wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, something not many motorcycles out there are capable of. There is new switchgear on deck, alongside a cooled phone compartment with USB-C charging,
Without affecting the bike's original dimensions and overall stance, Triumph also revised the bodywork of the new Tiger, changing the lines and appearance of the fuel tank, radiator cowls, beak and windscreen. There is a new LED headlight up front, complete with cornering functionality.
Triumph plans to offer the 2027 Tiger 1200 in four different versions, namely GT Pro, Rally Pro, GT Explorer and Rally Explorer. Setting them apart are, among other things, the size of the fuel tank, the choice of wheels, various protective components, and the riding position.
There are also different colors to be had depending on the model. Triumph already lists the five new two-wheelers on its configurators, complete with pricing information. Important to note is the fact that, despite the many changes that made it into the design, the price for the new versions is not significantly higher than the 2024 incarnations.
Photo: Triumph You can read all about pricing and available colors in the lines below, but before you do that, I should also mention the new rides will be available at dealers from December 2026.
2027 Triumph Tiger 1200 GT Pro (Sapphire Black, Aluminum Silver/Pacific Blue) - $22,995 2027 Triumph Tiger 1200 Rally Pro (Matt Khaki Green, Ash Grey) - $24,445 2027 Triumph Tiger 1200 GT Explorer (Aluminum Silver/Pacific Blue, Granite) - $24,995 2027 Triumph Tiger 1200 Rally Explorer (Ash Grey/Sapphire Black, Matt Khaki Green) - $26,445
Triumph presented the new Tiger 1200 a few days before the largest motorcycle show in the world, the Esposizione Internazionale Ciclo Motociclo e Accessori (EICMA), opens its doors in Milan, Italy, next week. The bike maker will attend the event, and it will probably bring this new bike along.
autoevolution will be on location at the Fiera Milano Rho to bring you all the hottest bikes and moto technologies to be presented there, including the ones made by Triumph. Toyota Puts Snow Tracks on Five SUVs and Trucks, Unloads Them at SEMA 2026 as the Snowhunter Bunch
13 photos
Photo: Toyota
It's not long now until the 2026 edition of the SEMA show opens its doors in Las Vegas, and you all know what that means: the craziest and wackiest of ideas will take center stage, aiming to surprise, delight, and shock. Among them, five Toyota SUVs and trucks equipped with snow tracks so they don't get stuck in the white powder.
A few days before SEMA opens its doors, Japanese carmaker Toyota revealed a few images and some details of what it calls the Snowhunter concepts. That would be a small group of badass Toyotas (Tundra, Tacoma, 4Runner, Land Cruiser, and Sequoia) made even more so by the removal of their wheels and the fitting of tracks, along with other bits of equipment.
Toyota says the lineup is meant to imagine how each of these vehicles could be equipped so they can be used for winter exploration, no matter how much snow is lying around. Naturally, the tracks are not the only changes made.
Imagined by the carmaker together with its North American design studio, CALTY Design Research. Their defining trait are the tracks that make the connection to the ground, but for them to be fitted, a lot more changes had to be made.
Photo: Toyota Among them, the fitting of lift components sourced from Toyota Genuine Parts and TRD (Toyota Racing Development). This change is accompanied by a specific camouflage and badging across the five models, gloss-black accents here and there, and Rigid lighting solutions. Here's what each of the five models has to offer.
Toyota Tundra Snowhunter Concept The Japanese pickup truck was imagined as a sort of mobile basecamp for remote expeditions. Sure, it does wear snow tracks, but it's not these things that make it special. What does that is something called the TrailLift Pro Rack System. Meant for the truck's bed, it relies on a configurable frame to turn it into a flexible platform that can carry everything the owner might imagine: bikes, kayaks, canoes, and other heavy gear.
The system can be used to store, organize, and manage gear, and it comes with an articulated top rack that lowers to make loading easier. Elsewhere on the truck, Toyota fitted TRD rear billet control arms, a Predator step, and a bunch of extra lights.
Toyota Tacoma Snowhunter Concept A more trail-oriented Snowhunter concept is the one based on the Tacoma pickup. It, too, propped on snow tracks, it packs a lot of adventure gear, including some that you don't necessarily need or get to use on snow alone: a roof rack, full-length bed rack with MOLLE panels, awning, cargo storage, recovery equipment, and bed lighting.
Photo: Toyota Toyota says this version has been made in such a way as to travel tight trails, especially in changing conditions, including on winter routes that would otherwise be inaccessible for the standard Tacoma.
Toyota 4Runner Snowhunter Concept Moving into SUV land, the Snowhunter family starts with the 4Runner -based version, made in such a way as to be able to travel trails that have not been plowed. To do that, it gets extra protection around and beneath the bodywork.
For this design, Toyota went for rock rails, a Prinsu roof rack with accessory panels, and a Thule Pulse 2 cargo box that also extends its carrying capabilities and increases its chances of surviving a rough trail.
Toyota Land Cruiser Snowhunter Concept Toyota's most iconic SUV did not escape the carmaker's SEMA effort, so it too got a quartet of tracks. On top of that, the vehicle was also fitted with rock rails and skid plates to protect it from harm, and a Prinsu roof rack complete with accessory panels.
Photo: Toyota Wearing the same overalls as its siblings, the Land Cruiser throws in something the others do not offer: a Thule SnowPack ski rack capable of transporting the precious gear that allows people to have fun on snowy slopes.
Toyota Sequoia Snowhunter Concept The large Japanese SUV gets the SEMA treatment in pretty much the same fashion as the others, carrying extras the likes of the a TRD front skid plate, cast aluminum running boards, a Prinsu roof rack with accessory panels, and a Thule Pulse 2 cargo box.
All of you who can make the trip to Las Vegas next week will get to see all five Toyota Snowhunters on display at the Las Vegas Convention Center. There's a good chance this is the only time the general public gets to see the concepts in the metal, as they'll probably drop off the radar for good after that.
These are, like most of the other designs to be shown during the event by most of the participating companies, just special project prototype vehicles, and there are no plans in place to send them into production. They might inspire people, though, into making the changes themselves so that they mimic the capabilities of these rides.

2027 Dodge Charger Gets Special-Edition Package Celebrating 90 Years of Mopar
7 photos
Photo: Stellantis
The 2026 SEMA Show is just around the corner, and, unsurprisingly, Mopar joins the event to showcase a new special-edition package. It's called Exclusive Mopar '27, celebrates 90 years of Mopar "passion, performance, and personalization," and graces two versions of the 2027 Dodge Charger.
The package is available on the Charger R/T and Scat Pack Plus, both two-door coupes with turbocharged inline-six powerplants. Regardless of the choice, customers will get carbon-fiber upgrades like a front splitter, a rear spoiler, and a carbon-fiber hood.
The lightweight hood includes a functional scoop, while the cars will have a unique graphics package. Exclusive Mopar '27 will be limited to three exterior colors, Bludicrous, Diamond Black, and White Knuckle.
Based on the only official photo available as of this writing, the black and white cars will get blue stripes, while the blue Charger will get black stripes. The bundle will also include a limited-series plaque mounted under the hood and a unique badge on the dashboard. Speaking of which, Mopar wants to produce only 270 units.
And I'm not talking about 270 examples each; that's the total for both the R/T and Scat Pack Plus. The production will be split into 90 vehicles offered in each of the three exterior colors. Exactly 243 of these cars will be sold in the United States, with the remaining 27 examples available in Canada. Production will begin in the spring of 2027. Dealer orders begin in early January 2027.
How much does it cost to add the Exclusive Mopar '27 bundle to a Charger? The package costs $10,995. That's a 20% premium for the Charger R/T, which comes in at $49,995 before options. All told, the R/T with the said bundle will set you back $60,990 before you start adding other options. The Scat Pack Plus model starts from $59,990, which means you'll pay a total of $70,985 to take it home with the limited-edition Mopar treatment.
The Mopar '27 package will make an appearance at the 2026 SEMA Show , but it will actually debut a few days earlier. Stellantis will introduce it at the Mopar NHRA Las Vegas Nationals at the Las Vegas Motor Speedway on October 30. The cars will be on display through November 1. You'll then be able to see them at the Las Vegas Convention Center between November 3 and 6.
Mopar '27 is the 15th annual package introduced around the SEMA Show since 2011. There should be 16, but the 2020 edition was cancelled due to the Covid-19 pandemic. The series began with the Charger in 2011, with the nameplate returning in 2015 and 2023. The 300, Dart, Challenger, Durango, Jeep Gladiator, and Ram also received similar treatments over the years.
As a brief reminder, the 2027 Dodge Charger R/T comes with a twin-turbo, 3.0-liter inline-six (SIXPACK) setup good for 420 horsepower. It hits 60 mph in 4.6 seconds and runs the quarter-mile in 12.9 clicks. The Scat Pack Plus model has larger turbochargers, standard AWD, and packs 550 horsepower. Hitting 60 mph takes only 3.9 seconds, toward a quarter-mile run of 12.2 seconds.

Deposco ’s Q3 2026 Commerce Signal report found that parcel carrier rates fell 3.3% from the second quarter, but what companies actually paid per package fell only 0.6%. Heavier packages, faster shipping services, and more residential deliveries ate into those savings.
What’s Related
The report draws on shipping, sales, and inventory activity flowing through Deposco’s software . The company says its platform serves more than 4,900 supply chain operators, accounting for over $84 billion in annual merchandise sales and 485 million orders.
“Rates came down, but operators didn’t feel it. That’s the story of the quarter,” said Eric Lemus, vice president of strategy and data analytics at Deposco.
“Every margin conversation we’re having right now comes back to what actually shipped. That’s where the money went and where operators should focus.”
RELATED: USPS Plans Peak Rate Hikes for Heavy, Long-Distance Packages | Peak Season Outlook Brightens as 52% Expect More Freight Activity
Why there is so little savings
Deposco compared what it would cost to ship the same mix of packages in both quarters with what companies actually paid. Rates fell, but companies shipped heavier packages and used more expensive delivery services, leaving them with little savings.
That distinction helps explain the quarter’s results. Lower rates offered some relief, but changes in package weight, delivery speed, and destination ate into the savings. The report also cited regional carriers raising fees.
Costs remained higher than a year earlier. Deposco reported that actual parcel costs per package were up 6.9% year over year, despite the small quarterly decline.
Orders grew as inventory caught up
Order growth stood at 5.3% year over year at the quarter’s close, while gross merchandise value, the dollar value of goods sold, grew 11.7%. Average order value increased 4.1%.
Inventory also rose late in the quarter. Median days of inventory on hand reached 93, up from 88 in mid-September and level with the same period last year. The increase closed a year-over-year inventory gap during the final three weeks of September.
The findings reflect activity among Deposco customers, not the entire shipping market. Deposco says the data is aggregated and anonymized, and its figures are approximate.
Expect a more expensive peak season
Deposco expects per-package costs to rise during the holiday shipping season , pointing to peak surcharges and renewed pressure from fuel prices.
The company also revisited its July prediction that parcel inflation would keep climbing during the third quarter. Rates instead declined, and Deposco said the new report explains the missed forecast and changes to its methods.
“Shipping costs cooled during Q3. But get ready for an expensive peak season,” the report stated.

The Ming underground mine, Newfoundland and Labrador. Credit: FireFly Metals
Posted By: Henry Lazenby October 27, 2026
FireFly Metals (TSX, ASX: FFM) has found a new copper-gold system near its idle Nugget Pond mill in Newfoundland, adding a potential satellite deposit to its Green Bay development plans.
Hole FFR26-071 at Mount Joy cut 22.5 metres grading 1.87% copper and 0.64 gram gold per tonne from 109 metres downhole. The prospect is 35 km east of the Ming mine, the main Green Bay deposit, which is about 360 km northwest of St. John’s.
“We view the discovery as an encouraging early indication of the regional exploration potential at Green Bay, with several additional targets yet to be tested,” BMO Capital Markets analyst Rene Cartier wrote in a note Tuesday.
The discovery, just 2.6 km from Nugget Pond, gives FireFly another target to test alongside its proposed Ming restart and expansion. A larger regional resource base could support more production over a longer mine life, although Mount Joy’s size and economics have yet to be established and the company has yet to establish how it might fit into its development plans.
Shares gained 9.2% to $1.42 by midday in Toronto, valuing FireFly at about $1.32 billion (US$941 million). The stock closed 9.3% higher in Sydney at A$1.41.
Shallow discovery
The Mount Joy intercept included nine metres grading 2.95% copper and 0.95 gram gold from 112 metres. The initial hole, FFR26-064, returned 6.45 metres grading 0.81% copper and 1.19 grams gold from 15.55 metres downhole.
A survey inside the first hole identified a conductive target about 80 metres to the south, leading FireFly to drill FFR26-071. Such surveys measure electrical conductivity to help locate sulphide bodies beyond a drill hole.
Follow-up hole FFR26-076 cut about 40 metres of semi-massive sulphides between 240 and 280 metres downhole. Assays are pending and expected within about four weeks. Visual sulphides alone don’t establish metal grades or economic value.
The company interprets a fault between the mineralization in the latter two holes. More conductive targets remain to be tested and FireFly plans a winter access road from Nugget Pond to support drilling early next year.
FireFly described Mount Joy as a volcanogenic massive sulphide, or VMS, system with characteristics similar to Ming and Tilt Cove. It lies along the same geological contact as the former Tilt Cove mine.
Restart plans
FireFly has budgeted $16.7 million for regional exploration in fiscal 2027, with three surface rigs working across its targets. An initial resource for the separate Main Mine prospect, less than 3 km from Ming, is due in the first quarter.
Six underground rigs are converting and expanding Ming’s resources ahead of an updated estimate and feasibility study due in the first quarter of 2027. FireFly expects to consider a final investment decision around mid-year and targets copper production in 2029.
The Green Bay inferred resource published in August totals 60.2 million measured and indicated tonnes grading 1.9% copper and 0.5 gram gold, containing about 1.16 million tonnes of copper and 908,000 oz. gold. The total includes Ming and Little Deer.
An August preliminary economic assessment outlined a base case processing 1.8 million tonnes annually over more than 32 years. Newfoundland and Labrador has approved selected early works, including clearing and a construction camp. Electrical and wastewater-treatment upgrades are underway.
“In our view, continued exploration success, and growth in resources, will further support FireFly’s investment case for an upscaled centralized processing facility with higher production rates over a longer mine life,” Cartier wrote.

Seoul police have booked 80 people for using aftermarket devices to switch on Tesla’s “Full Self-Driving” in cars that aren’t allowed to run it in South Korea. Officers also seized 21 of the devices.
The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency announced the case on Tuesday. It’s the largest enforcement action yet against the FSD “jailbreak” hardware that has spread through China, Europe, and Korea over the past year.
Police say the suspects either imported the unlock modules from Europe and China or made their own. One plugged a European-made unit into his own Tesla. Another, an IT worker, built his device with information he found on GitHub.
Suspects also swapped advice online on how to unlock FSD and how to stop the car from keeping any record that it had been activated.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
They’re charged under Korea’s Motor Vehicle Management Act, which bans unauthorized software changes that can affect a vehicle’s safety. The penalty is up to two years in prison or a fine of up to 20 million won (about $15,000).
The Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport asked police to look into it back in April after finding signs of unauthorized activation. A police official told Korea JoongAng Daily that “safety risks were confirmed,” including the possibility of FSD misreading driving conditions. The investigation is ongoing, with police consulting the ministry and the Korea Transportation Safety Authority on the technical side.
Most Korean Teslas can’t legally run FSD
Tesla launched FSD (Supervised) in South Korea in late 2025, but only on US-built vehicles: Model S, Model X, and Cybertruck. Those cars are exempt from Korean safety certification under the Korea-US free trade agreement. The Model 3 and Model Y, which Tesla ships to Korea from Giga Shanghai, haven’t cleared Korea’s safety standards for the feature.
And those two models are the bulk of the fleet. Citing Carisyou Data Lab, Korea JoongAng Daily reports that 47,458 of the 229,311 Teslas on Korean roads as of August, or 20.7%, can legally use FSD.
That number doesn’t match the government’s own count from a few months earlier. In May, data released by lawmaker Park Yong-gap showed just 4,292 of 180,684 registered Teslas (2.4%) were eligible: 2,708 Model X, 1,193 Model S, and 391 Cybertruck. Either way, the vast majority of Korean Tesla owners can’t legally use FSD, and some of them paid over $6,000 for it anyway .
The hardware is the same, which is why the hack works. The modules plug into the car’s CAN bus and get around the regional software lock.
Tesla has been fighting the devices itself. In April, it started remotely detecting them and stripping FSD from affected cars, warned owners they’d be fully liable for any crash and could lose warranty coverage, and permanently banned some Chinese owners from FSD.

GM Forgot a Part: 2026 Cadillac CT5-V Blackwings Delivered Missing Precision Package Hardware
12 photos
Photo: Cadillac
General Motors has issued a Customer Satisfaction Program bulletin, not an actual recall, because certain 2026 Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing examples equipped with the $18,000 Precision Package were actually delivered to customers missing critical rear suspension toe links. It sounds like an "oops" moment in which a GM employee failed to do their job.
The Precision Package is designed to significantly sharpen the sedan’s track capabilities by adding stiffer springs, a larger front stabilizer bar, revised suspension bushings, upgraded steering knuckles, and carbon-ceramic brakes to match the extra oomph.
However, it turns out that General Motors delivered cars missing critical components. A specific part of the $18,000 package was left out. Two rear suspension toe-link assemblies (Part no. 85829248) and four mounting bolts are missing. They were originally meant to be installed by dealership technicians during the Pre-Delivery Inspection (PDI).
These supplementary track-performance parts were supposed to be shipped loose, placed inside the trunk of the Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing sedan, upon delivery from the GM Lansing Grand River Assembly plant in Michigan, but were entirely omitted from the affected vehicles.
Photo: Cars and Bids Because these specific toe links are intended as an uninstalled, track-focused extra, General Motors' remedy does not involve taking the car to a dealership to have the technicians install them onto the suspension. Owners can have them installed at a service shop or ask the dealership technicians to do it.
The program is completely free of charge to affected owners and will remain active through October 31, 2028. Because the $18,000 Precision Package is a highly specialized, track-focused option, the overall production numbers are quite low.
This means that only a handful of early-delivery 2026 models left the factory without the aluminum performance toe links. The Customer Satisfaction Program bulletin affects just 11 units in the United States.
So what does the Precision Package actually bring? The Precision Package is a hardcore, track-focused chassis overhaul, designed for drivers who want to rock the track in their almighty Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing high-performance sedan, with no interference with the engine.
The package, however, completely changes how the car handles extreme cornering and full loads and costs $18,000 on top of the $100,695 starting price of the CT5-V Blackwing with the manual transmission or $106,970 when the automatic transmission is involved.
Photo: Cars and Bids For the money, it brings a stiffer suspension with increased spring rates, a larger front stabilizer bar, and heavily revised suspension bushings. New steering knuckles and rear suspension toe links, the parts that are currently missing from the trunks, are also on the menu.
The Magnetic Ride Control dampers, electronic limited-slip differential, and steering systems are uniquely calibrated to match the hardware, while the carbon-ceramic brakes massively reduce unsprung weight, delivering fade-free, mighty stopping power even under track abuse.
With or without the package, the engine specs remain unchanged. This means that the 6.2-liter supercharged LT4 V8 pushes out 668 horsepower (677 metric horsepower) and 659 pound-feet (893 Newton meters) of torque.
That is what pushes it from zero to hero (0 to 60 mph or 0 to 97 kph) in 3.4 seconds when equipped with the ten-speed auto box or 3.6 seconds when it comes with the six-speed manual transmission.
It runs the quarter mile in 11.4 seconds with a trap speed of 128 mph (206 kph) on its way to a top speed of over 200 mph (322 kph). Those numbers have always made it a formidable rival for the German sports sedan segment, like the BMW M5 or the discontinued Mercedes-AMG E 63.

For a small carrier, the choice of whether to own a trailer, finance one, run power only, or rent by the day looks like a simple equipment question, but it is really a business decision with a cost structure attached to every option, and getting that math wrong is one of the quietest and most expensive mistakes a growing fleet can make, which is the thread that ran through a recent Long Haul conversation recorded at F3 in Chattanooga with Matt Harb, Vice President of Product and Operations at the trailer-sharing marketplace Repowr.
Harb spends his days on the phone with owner-operators and small fleets, and he said the point of those calls is to understand what is actually weighing on them, from fuel costs to how they are landing and keeping customers. What he keeps hearing underneath all of it is that the trailer, the so-called dumb box behind the truck, quietly dictates which loads a carrier can and cannot take. That is the problem Repowr is built to solve, and the way Harb talks about it reframes the trailer from a thing you buy into a lever you pull only when the business case is there.
The Long Haul at F3 https://t.co/52zNusl6tZ — FreightWaves (@FreightWaves) October 27, 2026
An Airbnb For Trailers
Repowr runs what amounts to a marketplace for trailers, and the comparison Harb reached for is one most people will recognize immediately, an Airbnb-style rental experience built for freight. Large and midsize fleets list excess equipment they are not fully using, and owner-operators and small fleets rent it by the day, drawing from what the company calls its Universal Trailer Network. Harb said there are roughly 3,500 trailers on the platform at any given moment across the country, spanning dry vans, reefers, and flatbeds, and the pitch is that this is good, current equipment rather than a yard full of beat-up 25-year-old boxes.
The mechanics are deliberately low-friction. A carrier can rent for as little as three days or as long as 90 days or more, pick a trailer up in one place and drop it in another, and in many cases find a replacement waiting where the last one was returned. Harb said the platform leans on data about each carrier so it only surfaces trailers that operator is actually qualified to rent, which keeps people out of the frustrating cycle of chasing listings they will never get approved for. The fastest-growing group he sees is carriers building a fleet from scratch, people who would rather put their capital into trucks and their team than into depreciating trailers, and who use rentals to cover the equipment side while they scale.
The Real Cost Of Power Only
Plenty of carriers already solve the trailer problem by running power only, pulling someone else’s equipment and skipping the asset entirely, and Harb was candid that there is a real trade in that choice. Power-only freight tends to pay below drop-and-hook work, and he pegged the gap on most load boards at somewhere in the range of five to ten percent. More than the rate, though, what a carrier gives up is control, because power only tends to pin a truck into a region and tie its next move to wherever the equipment has to go rather than to the highest-paying lane on the board.
I described the version of that trap I used to hate as an operator, picking up a towaway in Chattanooga that had to end up in the Northeast and then having to position myself around getting the equipment back instead of chasing the best freight. Harb agreed that the regional lock-in is still real, and said it is part of why Repowr rolled out what it calls short-run pricing. For rentals under 14 days, a carrier can often get a trailer at close to half the usual cost, in some cases around eight dollars a day, because suppliers want their equipment repositioned quickly and are willing to trade price for speed. It is a rare arrangement where the carrier and the trailer owner both come out ahead.
Drop And Hook, And The Trailer Ratio Nobody Explains
The deeper point Harb kept circling back to is that the money in a lot of markets lives in drop-and-hook freight, and drop-and-hook requires trailer availability that most small carriers simply do not have. He estimated that something like half of all freight runs through drop-and-hook, which means a carrier without spare trailers is quietly boxed out of a large share of the most profitable, repeatable lanes. When a shipper asks for a two-to-one or three-to-one trailer-to-truck ratio, the small operator who cannot float that many trailers has to walk away, even though access to rented equipment would let them say yes.
Both Harb and I were clear that this is where small carriers misread what scaling actually means. Growth is not simply buying another truck and then another truck, it is building the capacity to source more trailers so the trucks behind them stay loaded, because the margin lives in the box, not just the tractor. Harb acknowledged the mental hurdle, that the first time an operator leaves a trailer sitting on a shipper’s yard it almost breaks the logic in their head, and he said it is not the right move for a one-truck operation. Once a carrier climbs into the five-to-ten-truck range and is genuinely building a business, though, he argued it is time to start thinking about dropping and hooking, usually beginning with a two-to-one ratio before working up to anything larger.
Matching The Asset To The Commitment
If there is a single business-structure mistake Harb finds hardest to watch, it is carriers matching a long-term asset to a short-term or uncertain opportunity. He described talking to a 15-truck fleet that was about to sign long-term leases on reefers because a few shippers were dangling promising lanes, and his reaction was that a promise of freight is exactly the wrong reason to take on years of fixed equipment cost. Rent for three months, see whether the lanes are real, and only then consider buying something to own forever. The excitement of the next big thing, he said, is what pushes operators of every size to pour long-term capital into a decision they may regret within months, often with no clean way out.
The economics behind that caution are not subtle. Harb put a used dry van trailer at around 35,000 dollars and a new one near 55,000, and reminded listeners that the sticker is only the beginning once insurance, a place to park it, maintenance, and the cost of moving it empty are added in. Repositioning a trailer through a traditional loadout service can run 500 to 600 dollars a trip. By contrast, Repowr charges on a rolling 30-day basis, so a carrier who needs 14 days pays for 14 days, with no sunk cost anywhere in the equation, which is the piece Harb kept emphasizing. The minute you buy a trailer or sign a long lease, you own a depreciating asset whether it is earning or not.
Watch For The Scam, And Know The Sign-Up
Harb was also direct about a problem Repowr itself has written about, the trailer-rental scams increasingly aimed at owner-operators. His rules of thumb were plain. Never send money by a cash app to pull a trailer out of some yard, treat a deal that looks too good to be true as exactly that, and remember that criminals are now spoofing websites and lifting real company branding to look legitimate. If a listing seems impossibly cheap, like a trailer for 180 dollars over three months, rethink it before showing up to claim it. The single best defense he offered costs nothing, which is to pick up the phone and talk to a human to confirm the operation is real before sending anyone anywhere.
On the legitimate side, he walked through how onboarding works, and the friction is low by design. A carrier enters its DOT number, and roughly 85 percent pass the initial screen, then uploads a license and a couple of documents through an integration that pulls much of the data automatically, a process that takes about six minutes. Operators only see listings they are likely to be approved for, filling out a rental takes about seven minutes, and the platform includes a tool that lets a carrier type in its insurance agent, send the request, and have the two required certificates of insurance with additional-insured language handled on their behalf. Harb said about 85 percent of pickups happen the same day or the next, and that Repowr sets a floor on who gets on, requiring at least three months of active revenue and screening out the bottom 10 to 15 percent of operators, because the trailers belong to someone else and protecting that equipment is part of keeping suppliers willing to list.
Why It Matters
For a small carrier, equipment is one of the largest fixed costs in the business, and the difference between owning, leasing, running power only, and renting by the day is not a preference but a math problem that decides how much freight a fleet can profitably take. Treating the trailer as a flexible, on-demand resource rather than a permanent purchase lets a growing operation chase drop-and-hook lanes and spare capacity without locking into a depreciating asset, which is why flexibility has quietly become a competitive advantage, and why knowing its price is now part of running the business well.
